::: {#explain .lx-sec}
::: {.lx-sec-h}
## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="cost-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Four costs</dt><dd>Building the plant, fixed upkeep, fuel and upkeep per MWh; wind and solar are mostly building cost, gas plants mostly fuel.</dd>
<dt>Discounting</dt><dd>Money later is worth less than money now, so future costs and sales are divided by (1 + r) for every year of waiting.</dd>
<dt>WACC</dt><dd>The blended rate a project pays its lenders and owners; it is the discount rate of the plant.</dd>
<dt>Capital recovery factor</dt><dd>The share of the building cost to repay each year so that it is paid off, with interest, over the plant's life.</dd>
<dt>LCOE</dt><dd>The steady price per MWh that repays every cost over the life: yearly costs divided by yearly MWh, plus fuel and upkeep per MWh.</dd>
<dt>Tornado chart</dt><dd>Each input swung from low to high, one at a time, to rank what moves the result over the chosen ranges.</dd>
<dt>LCOE's blind spot</dt><dd>It gives every MWh the same worth, whatever the hour; what a MWh saves depends on when it arrives.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>The LCOE formula and the capital recovery factor</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

Paying off a building cost $C$ (\$/kW) with $n$ equal yearly payments $A$ at a real rate $r$ means the payments' present value equals $C$:

$$C = \sum_{t=1}^{n} \frac{A}{(1+r)^t} = A\,\frac{1-(1+r)^{-n}}{r} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad A = \underbrace{\frac{r}{1-(1+r)^{-n}}}_{\text{CRF}}\; C .$$

When $r = 0$ the CRF is simply $1/n$. The [LCOE]{.lx-term term="lcoe"} is the steady price $p$ at which the plant's discounted sales repay everything, so its net present value is zero. With $E = \mathrm{CF} \times 8{,}760 / 1{,}000$ MWh made per kW each year (the [capacity factor]{.lx-term term="capacity-factor"} from [lesson 5](index.html#lesson-5)):

$$\mathrm{LCOE} = \frac{\mathrm{CRF}\cdot C + \mathrm{FOM}}{E} + \text{heat rate}\times\text{gas price} + \mathrm{VOM}.$$

Check it on the wind farm: $\mathrm{CRF}(4\%, 30) = 0.05783$, so $0.05783 \times 1{,}712 + 34.57 = 133.58$ \$/kW each year; $E = 0.338 \times 8.76 = 2.961$ MWh per kW; $133.58 / 2.961 = \$45.11$ per MWh. The 2025 ATB writes the same equation with a fixed charge rate, $\mathrm{FCR} = \mathrm{CRF} \times$ a factor for taxes and depreciation; here that factor is 1.

The WACC blends what lenders and owners are paid. With a share $d$ of loans at rate $r_d$, owners' money at $r_e$ and tax rate $\tau$, the usual after-tax form is $d\,r_d(1-\tau) + (1-d)\,r_e$; the step left the tax out. A nominal rate $n$ becomes real with $(1+n) = (1+r)(1+i)$ for inflation $i$.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>Where LCOE's pieces go in a planning model</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

A planning model does not compare LCOEs. It charges each MW it builds a yearly cost $\mathrm{CRF}\cdot C + \mathrm{FOM}$, charges every MWh its fuel and upkeep, and chooses how much to build and how to run it hour by hour in one optimization. Value and cost then meet inside the model, which is how the timing problem of step 8 is handled.

- Capacity expansion with representative days (M3, upcoming in the Modeler tier) uses exactly this yearly charge.
- Techno-economic analysis inside an optimization model (M11, upcoming) adds taxes, credits and a boundary choice.
- Year-by-year cash flows, NPV, IRR and payback for one project are the Analyst lesson A1 (upcoming).

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper</span>What this calculator leaves out</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
<ul>
<li>Taxes, depreciation and tax credits: the agencies include them, so their LCOEs differ from these.</li>
<li>Interest paid during construction, and the time a plant takes to build.</li>
<li>Grid connection, new transmission, and the backup or balancing a variable plant may need.</li>
<li>Output that falls as equipment ages, and costs that differ by region.</li>
<li>Any change in costs over time: every input is one fixed number that you can move.</li>
<li>Step 8 counts only running-cost savings; a plant's worth also includes the capacity it offers at the peak.</li>
</ul>
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="c7-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="lowest" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “The plant with the lowest LCOE is always the cheapest choice for the grid.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. LCOE leaves out when and where the MWh arrive; on Prairie Town's hottest day a wind MWh saved $56.35 and a solar MWh $50.27.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="rate" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “The discount rate is a technical detail that barely changes the answer.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. From 4% to 7% real, the wind farm's LCOE rises from $45.11 to $58.27 per MWh, by 29.2%.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="tornado" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A tornado chart shows how likely each outcome is.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It shows how far the result moves over ranges someone chose, one input at a time; other ranges can change the ranking.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="cf" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “With the same building cost, a windier site gives a lower LCOE.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact. The same yearly cost is spread over more MWh: at a 43% capacity factor instead of 33.8%, wind's LCOE falls from $45.11 to $35.46.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="c7">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="calc" data-answer="c">
<p class="lx-qtext">A plant's yearly repayment plus fixed upkeep is $130 per kW. Each kW makes 2.628 MWh a year (a 30% capacity factor), and it burns no fuel. What is its LCOE?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">$13.00/MWh</li><li data-value="b">$39.00/MWh</li><li data-value="c">$49.47/MWh</li><li data-value="d">$130.00/MWh</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>$49.47/MWh: 130 ÷ 2.628 = 49.47. Yearly cost per kW divided by yearly MWh per kW.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="pv" data-answer="c">
<p class="lx-qtext">At 7% a year, what is $100 paid in 10 years worth today?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">$93.00</li><li data-value="b">$70.00</li><li data-value="c">$50.83</li><li data-value="d">$7.00</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>$50.83: 100 ÷ 1.07¹⁰ = 50.83. Each year of waiting divides by 1.07.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
```
:::

<div class="lx-card lx-real">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">In the real world</p>
<p>A levelized cost and a system's cost can move in opposite directions. In my study of a wind farm with hydrogen equipment, a higher hydrogen price led the optimizer to build a larger electrolyzer: its cost per kilogram rose, while the whole system's net cost fell (<a href="https://doi.org/10.1115/1.4063971">Journal of Mechanical Design, 2024</a>).</p>
</div>
